# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterised by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature during selective coronary angiography in the absence of significant obstructive epicardial disease. It was first described by Tambe, Demany, Zimmerman and Mascarenhas in 1972 as a new angiographic finding linking angina pectoris to slow flow velocity of dye in coronary arteries. Since then it has been recognised as an independent clinical entity, also termed coronary slow flow syndrome, syndrome Y, or primary coronary slow flow. It is variously called 'CSFP', 'coronary slow flow syndrome', 'syndrome Y', or "primary" coronary slow flow, and importantly should be distinguished from delayed contrast progression in the context of reperfusion therapy or other secondary causes such as coronary ectasia, spasm, valvular heart disease, or connective tissue disorders.

The phenomenon was originally assessed qualitatively, but quantification became standardised through the corrected Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count (CTFC). Although the TIMI flow grade is a valuable and widely used qualitative measure, it is limited by its subjective and categorical nature; Gibson and colleagues therefore counted the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardised distal landmarks to objectively assess coronary blood flow as a continuous variable, and the method proved reproducible. Because the left anterior descending artery is longer, its frame count is corrected by dividing by 1.7 to derive the CTFC. The currently adopted diagnostic criteria, proposed by Beltrame in 2012, define CSFP as delayed distal opacification in the absence of significant epicardial stenosis (≤40%), with a TIMI flow grade of 2 or a CTFC greater than 27 frames in one or more epicardial vessels.

## Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation

CSFP is an uncommon but underrecognised finding. It has an incidence of 1–5% in patients undergoing coronary angiography and is most frequently found in young men who are smokers with metabolic syndrome. In a study seeking to define its prevalence and clinical features, 1,741 consecutive patients who underwent angiography were screened, and those with normal ejection fraction and normal coronary arteries were included. Clinically, the entity is far from benign. It is a frequent finding typically observed in patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes; although known to interventional cardiologists for decades, the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear, and the clinical implications are significant, with over 80% of patients experiencing recurrent chest pain and considerable impairment in quality of life. Affected individuals commonly present with anginal symptoms including resting and exertional chest pain, and while overall mortality is low, accumulating evidence highlights a correlation with life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and recurrent syncope. Indeed, CSFP has been linked to QT prolongation and arrhythmic risk. A reported case describes recurrent syncope with normalisation of flow after intracoronary adenosine, multiple episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on Holter monitoring with increased QTc dispersion, and a good response to oral dipyridamole.

## Pathophysiology

The mechanisms underlying CSFP remain incompletely understood, but microvascular and endothelial dysfunction are central. Small vessel dysfunction has been implicated in the pathogenesis of CSFP since its first description, with investigators reporting fibromuscular hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial oedema, thickening and degeneration in coronary microvessels. Mangieri and colleagues found thickening of vessel walls with luminal size reduction, mitochondrial abnormalities, and reduced glycogen content in left ventricular endomyocardial biopsies. A landmark physiological study reframed the disorder as one of microvascular tone. Beltrame and colleagues indicated that CSFP was associated with a chronically elevated resting coronary microvascular tone characterised by low coronary sinus oxygen saturation and blunted responses to endothelial stimuli.

Endothelial dysfunction, particularly impaired nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability, features prominently. Microvascular abnormalities and endothelial dysfunction are thought to cause slow coronary flow, and studies have assessed plasma NO levels to determine their pathogenic role. Endothelial dysfunction plays a key role in the aetiopathogenesis even without obstructive lesions; reduced plasma endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) is an important indicator, and basal eNOS levels are lower in patients than controls with a more marked decrease after exercise. Genetic susceptibility may also contribute. In a study of 180 patients with CSFP and 87 controls, the allelic distribution of eNOS 894G/T was significantly associated with CSFP (odds ratio 1.58). Additional metabolic and inflammatory contributors have been described. Patients have raised plasma homocysteine and asymmetric dimethylarginine—an NO synthase inhibitor—and decreased adiponectin concentrations and paraoxonase activity, all markers of endothelial dysfunction.

## Relationship to Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction

CSFP is frequently equated with coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), though this relationship is debated. The Coronary Vasomotion Disorders International Study recommendations recognise CSFP (defined as corrected TFC > 27) as evidence of impaired microvascular function that can be equated to a diagnosis of CMD. However, invasive validation has produced conflicting results. Guidelines recommend that CSFP can diagnose CMD in patients with angina and non-obstructed coronary arteries, and CSFP has historically been regarded as a sign of coronary endothelial dysfunction. Delayed contrast progression without significant stenosis is observed in roughly 7% of angiograms, and CTFC more broadly serves as an angiographic surrogate for coronary blood flow. Newer wire-based studies caution against over-interpretation. CSF by invasive angiography is frequently understood to indicate CMD in patients with ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries, but the relationship between visual estimates of CSF and quantitative wire-based diagnosis of CMD is uncertain.

## Management

No definitive, guideline-endorsed therapy exists, but several agents targeting the microvasculature have shown benefit. Various medications have been evaluated, though efficacies are not well established; oral calcium channel blockers can attenuate the microvascular effects associated with slow flow, and intracoronary agents improve the TIMI frame count. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 80 patients with chest pain, normal coronary arteries and CSF defined by CTFC, randomly assigning them to diltiazem sustained-release capsules or placebo. Beta-blockers with NO-mediated vasodilator properties have also been studied. Slow coronary flow occurs without epicardial stenosis in patients with chest pain, there are no definite treatment modalities, and one study investigated nebivolol's effects on endothelial function and inflammatory markers. In that study, chest pain relief was detected in 38 of 42 patients (90%), and systolic and diastolic blood pressure and high-sensitivity CRP were significantly reduced. Mibefradil, a T-type calcium channel blocker, was assessed in one of the few prospective placebo-controlled trials. Beltrame and colleagues reported the angiographic and clinical benefits of mibefradil in CSFP, in one of the few placebo-controlled prospective trials, evaluating its effects in 20 patients in a randomised crossover design.

## Conclusion

CSFP is a clinically relevant angiographic disorder linking microvascular and endothelial dysfunction to recurrent angina, impaired quality of life, and occasional arrhythmic risk. Also known as cardiac syndrome Y, it is defined as delayed distal opacification of the coronary vasculature, and various hypotheses regarding its substrate—including microvascular and endothelial dysfunction—have been postulated. Standardisation of definitions and further mechanistic and randomised therapeutic studies are needed to refine diagnosis and management.
